name: Lethavex
description: Lethavex is a targeted amygdala-limbic suppressor designed to chemically interrupt acute grief responses without sedating the user or impairing cognitive function. It was developed and marketed as a 'bereavement productivity aid' — users can attend funerals in the morning and return to work by afternoon. The drug does not eliminate grief; it walls it off, leaving a muffled awareness that something is wrong without the debilitating weight of it.
effects: Suppression of acute grief and mourning responses
Maintained cognitive clarity and workplace functionality
Emotional distance from painful memories without memory loss
Reduced crying reflex and physical grief symptoms (chest tightness, nausea)
Mild emotional blunting across adjacent feelings
side_effects: Grief rebound effect upon cessation — sometimes more intense than original loss
Emotional blunting can persist 12-24 hours beyond dose window
Long-term use linked to complicated grief disorder — grief never fully processed
Dissociative episodes if used during active trauma rather than aftermath
Dependency risk in chronic users who fear confronting stored grief
Reported 'grief debt' phenomenon — suppressed feelings accumulate and discharge unpredictably
cultural_context: Lethavex is one of Lazarus's top-ten sellers by volume. In a society where bereavement leave is often measured in hours rather than weeks, it has become functionally normalized — workers are quietly expected to medicate their grief and return to productivity. Tier 2 workers use it to avoid losing shifts. Tier 3 professionals use it to avoid appearing weak in performance reviews. The drug has a dark cultural nickname on the Shelf: 'the coffin lid,' because people say it buries you with your dead.
story_hooks: A Tier 2 dockworker has been taking Lethavex daily for three years since losing their child — they've never actually grieved, and a street doc warns them that the accumulated 'grief debt' could trigger a catastrophic emotional break at any moment

A Lazarus whistleblower reveals internal studies showing the company knew about grief debt syndrome a decade before launch and buried the data — the story breaks just as a mass bereavement event hits the city

Someone running a grief support group on the Shelf notices that every member is on Lethavex — prescribed by the same corporate wellness clinic — and starts to wonder if the clinic is suppressing community solidarity as much as individual pain
